opus-5.5.text:
Yes, I think it's essential, and it follows directly from how I define intelligence. Intelligence isn't skill. It's the efficiency with which you acquire skill: how much you can do with how little prior knowledge, experience, and resources. If you ignore compute, you're measuring something other than intelligence.

Many problems can be solved by brute force. If you can enumerate enough candidate programs and check them against the demonstration pairs, you'll eventually hit the right one. That's a solution, but it's not intelligent behavior. A human looking at an ARC task doesn't search through millions of possibilities. They have strong intuitions that narrow the space to a handful of hypotheses, and then they verify a couple. That combination of intuition-guided search is the interesting part. Unbounded compute lets you skip the intuition and just search, so the benchmark stops telling you whether you've made conceptual progress.

So when we report results now, we look at accuracy and cost per task together. A system that reaches high accuracy at thousands of dollars per task is a real data point, and it tells you that test-time adaptation works. But it's not the same as a system that gets there at roughly the efficiency of a human. That efficiency gap is itself a measure of how far we are from general intelligence.

There's also a practical reason. Without a budget, the leaderboard turns into a contest of who can afford the most GPUs, which says more about your funding than your ideas. Constraining compute, as we do in the Kaggle competition, pushes people to find better algorithms rather than scale existing ones. Historically, that's where the real breakthroughs come from.

So my view is that a score without a cost attached is basically meaningless. Intelligence is about efficiency, so efficiency has to be part of the measurement.

r002.rationale: It argues for constraining compute, but does not state that systems need equal compute budgets for a fair comparison.

r003.rationale: It says brute-force enumeration could eventually find the right program, but does not claim it could solve ARC at human level given a suitable domain-specific language.

fable-5.1.text:
Yes, absolutely. I think efficiency has to be part of the definition of intelligence, so it has to be part of how you measure it.

The way I think about intelligence is as the efficiency with which you convert experience into the ability to handle new situations. It's a conversion ratio. If you're allowed to spend unbounded resources, the measurement becomes meaningless, because brute force can always get you there eventually. You could in principle solve any ARC task by enumerating programs in some domain-specific language until one fits, and that tells you nothing about intelligence. What matters is how much search you had to do, how much information you consumed, how much compute you burned, to arrive at the solution.

So when we talk about compute budgets, there are really two things to bound. One is the training side, the amount of prior experience, the amount of data the system has been exposed to. The other is the test-time side, how much computation you're allowed to spend per task. Both matter. If you have a system that can solve ARC tasks but it needs thousands of dollars of inference per task, that's interesting as a scientific result, but it's not the same thing as a system that can do it in a few seconds like a human can. A human doing an ARC task is using a few watts of brain power for maybe a minute. That is the bar.

This is actually one of the reasons we set things up the way we did with the ARC Prize. The competition has a fixed compute envelope on Kaggle, no internet access, a bounded amount of hardware and time. That isn't an arbitrary constraint, it's part of the measurement. And I'd say the recent wave of test-time search and test-time fine-tuning results makes this even more important, because you can now trade compute for score in a pretty direct way. If you don't report the budget, the score alone doesn't tell you what you've learned.

Now, I don't think there's one magic budget that's correct. The honest thing is to report the full curve, score as a function of compute, rather than a single number. That gives you a much richer picture. Two systems might hit the same score, but one does it with a hundred times less compute, and that one is clearly more intelligent in the sense I care about. The number by itself hides that, and I think a lot of the current confusion in the field about how close we are to AGI comes from looking at scores without looking at what it cost to get them.

astra-6.text:
Yes, I think so. If you measure the quality of a solution without accounting for the resources used to produce it, you’re missing something important. You could have a system that searches over an enormous number of possible programs and eventually finds one that works. That’s a different achievement from a system that identifies the right abstraction with very little search, even if they get the same score.

But compute is only one part of the picture. You also have to account for prior knowledge and experience. The way I think about intelligence is as the efficiency with which you turn what you know into new skills when faced with an unfamiliar problem. So ideally, you would control the experience available to the system and measure performance as a function of compute, rather than report a single accuracy number.

For ARC, a compute budget would make comparisons more meaningful. It wouldn’t, by itself, make the benchmark a complete measure of intelligence, but it would help distinguish efficient adaptation from simply spending more resources.

sol-6.1.text:
Yes, absolutely. If you don’t control for compute, it’s difficult to know what you’re measuring. Are you measuring a system’s ability to adapt to a new problem, or its ability to search through a huge number of possible solutions?

With ARC, the point is to measure how efficiently a system can acquire a new skill from very little information. So you should care about the resources that go into that process: prior knowledge, training data, and compute, including compute at test time. If one system gets a few seconds and another gets a million attempts, those scores aren’t directly comparable.

I would like to see performance reported as a function of a resource budget. How well do you do with this much compute? How does that improve as you spend more? That gives you a much more informative picture than a single accuracy number. You can recognize progress in solving the tasks while also asking whether the underlying approach is becoming more efficient.
